title: Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon
text: You have asked; How was the Mishnah written? If the Men of the Great Assembly first began writing it, and it was written down in increments by the Sages of each generation until Rebbe came and sealed it. Behold, most [of the Mishnah] is stated anonymously. And [the Talmud says that] the author of an anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir. And most of the Sages of the Talmud whose names are expressly mentioned - Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Shimon - were all students of Rabbi Akiva. And the Sages have taught us certain rules in the Talmud, that the Halachah goes like Rabbi Akiva when he disputes with one of his colleagues, and like Rabbi Yossi when he disputes with one of his colleagues. And all of them lived at the end of the Second Temple. And why, then, did the earlier Sages leave the greater part of this work for their successors to complete? The question becomes even more serious if nothing of the Mishnah was written until the end of Rebbe's time. Furthermore, if the sequence of the Orders [The six main divisions of the Mishnah] was organized in a systematic way, what is the reason of the order of the tractates [within each order]? For what reason was Yoma put before Shekalim, or Sukkah before Yom-Tov, and both of these before Rosh HaShanah? And why were other tractates, related in subject matter, not placed together: Another question concerns the Tosefta, of which we have heard that Rabbi Chiyya wrote it. Was it written after the sealing of the Mishnah, or concurrently with it? If the Tosefta was to include further matters that served to explicate the subjects of the Mishnah, why did Rebbe disregard these matters? Why didn't he write [the Tosefta] himself? After all, the Tosefta is taught in the names of the Sages of the Mishnah. Similarly, in what manner were the Beraitot composed, and how was the Talmud composed? And so to with the Savoraim, what is the chronology of the Sages after Ravina? And who was the authority after them, and how many years did these authorities reign from that time to the present:

Answer: So we have seen, with certainty that Rabbeinu Hakodesh ordered all six Orders of the Mishnah just as they are now learned, law after law, and one cannot add to or detract from them. Thus, we say in the Gemara, in Tractate Yevamos, chapter HaBa Al YeVimto "When was our Mishnah ordered'? During the days of Rebbe."...

And as for your question, "Why were the numerous Sages of the earlier generations disregarded for those of the later generations?" The earlier Sages were not disregarded. On the contrary, their statements were studied and all their opinions were taught. As it’s stated [in Pesachim] that when Hillel the Elder was appointed Nasi by the Sons of Besayra, he said to them: "Why did this happen to you, that I became nasi over you? Your laziness brought it about, because you did not serve the two greatest men of the time, Shemaya and Avtalyon....

This was the situation, the early Sages were not known by their names, rather the Nesi'im and the Heads of the Beit Din, because there were no disputes among them. Rather, all the explanations of the Torah, they knew clearly. They also knew the Talmud clearly, with all its details discussions and inferences. Thus, our Sages teach in Chapter Yesh Nachalin: Hillel the Elder had eighty students. Thirty of them were sufficiently worthy that the Divine Presence should rest upon them as it did upon Moses our teacher, thirty of them were sufficiently worthy that the sun should stand still for them as it did for Joshua bin Nun, and twenty were on an intermediate level between the other two. The greatest of all the students was Yonatan ben Uzziel, and the least of them was Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai. The Sages said about Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai that he did not neglect Bible and Mishna; Talmud; halakhot and aggadot; minutiae of the Torah and minutiae of the scribes; and the hermeneutical principles of the Torah with regard to a fortiori inferences; and verbal analogies; and the calculation of the calendric seasons; and numerical values of Hebrew letters [gimatriyot]; and parables of launderers, which are folktales that can be used to explain the Torah, and parables of foxes. In addition, he did not neglect esoteric matters, including the conversation of demons, and the conversation of palm trees, and the conversation of ministering angels, and more generally, a great matter and a small matter. A great matter is referring to the secrets of the Design of the Divine Chariot (see Ezekiel, chapter 1), the conduct of the transcendent universe, and a small matter is, for example, halakhot that were ultimately formulated in the framework of the discussions of Abaye and Rava. This informs you that even the discussions of Abbaye and Rava were not novel knowledge. Rather, [all such discussions] originate from the earlier Sages.
